(2019), already cited, supplies cluster/population allocation estimands under interference; it does not supply an emulation protocol, joint-neighborhood positivity diagnostics, or clone-censor rules that keep cluster strategies feasible. Buchanan et al. (Stat Med 2022; 10.1002/sim.9427) is the closest prior art: it defines a target-trial protocol for disseminated (spillover) effects of MOUD within provider-based clusters using routinely collected data, so the “rarely joined” claim should be read as rare rather than never. That paper is an application and estimation sketch under partial interference for a specific provider-cluster exposure mapping; it does not invent cluster-level clone-censor-weighting, does not resolve non-canonical exposure mappings, and does not evaluate network mismeasurement. Lu et al. (arXiv 2604.12900, 2026) propose emulating stepped-wedge cluster randomized trials for staggered policy adoption; that covers group-level policy emulation and mentions spillovers as a shared design concern, not individual-treatment cloning that assigns impossible joint strategies. Official TARGET resources (target-guideline.org, retrieved 2026) still scope the checklist to parallel-group, individually randomized target trials, list “Emulation of a cluster target trial” as a possible future extension, and state that no extensions are currently in development, which confirms rather than repairs the reporting gap. Contagion/homophily/spillover non-separability and joint-neighborhood positivity remain structural; sensitivity to edge deletion is proposed in the agenda and was not found as a standard TTE tool. Vote open: prior art proposes joins in narrow settings; none solves exposure-mapping canonicity, joint positivity, network error, or cluster-compatible cloning as stated.",

      "rationale": "Transport estimators (IOSW, outcome modeling, doubly robust/TMLE, calibration) are mature for trials and increasingly documented for observational sources; that is already acknowledged by the report’s Westreich citation and does not close the problem. The open core is accounting: transporting an observational estimate stacks treatment-exchangeability on sampling-exchangeability, both largely untestable, and no standard reporting practice decomposes a discrepancy between those failure modes. Scelo et al. (Front Epidemiol 2024; 10.3389/fepid.2024.1335241) explicitly lists the internal-validity and external-validity assumption blocks side by side, notes that most are untestable, and demonstrates TMLE transport from an observational birth cohort to a registry target; that formalizes the stack and does not provide joint sensitivity or attribution. Manke-Reimers et al. (Eur J Epidemiol 2025; 10.1007/s10654-025-01217-w), already cited, maps applied transport studies and underuse of flexible estimators; a scoping review of practice is evidence the gap remains, not a solution. Adamson et al. (Pharmacoepidemiol Drug Saf 2026; 10.1002/pds.70396) offers a stepwise transportability framework for comparative effectiveness and urges sensitivity for unmeasured effect modifiers, e-values, and tipping-point analyses; that is guidance and one-parameter sensitivity, not a joint compounding account that charges residual bias to confounding versus selection/effect-modification structure. Separate sensitivity tools for unmeasured confounding and for unmeasured selection/effect modification exist; they do not identify effects when both fail in correlated ways, and the discipline rule forbids treating sensitivity as solving identification. Causal representation learning for transport that preserves effect modification (rather than predictive invariance) remains workshop/early-methods work; no 2024–2026 applied TTE package (lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, TrialEmulation, zEpid) was found that ships joint internal-plus-external fragility bounds with attribution.       "rationale": "The problem is framed as a presentation/practice failure after standards already exist: a reader sees a bare hazard ratio and infers an intention-to-treat contrast, while the analysis estimated a censoring-weighted per-protocol effect among grace-period–compatible (often cloned) patients. Maringe et al. (IJE 2020; 10.1093/ije/dyaa057), already cited, already makes the CCW estimand type explicit; that formalizes the distinction and does not change what applied papers headline. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement (JAMA 2025; 10.1001/jama.2025.13350) require aligned objectives, estimands, and sensitivity analyses; TARGET item structure places target-trial protocol/estimand items (6a–g) beside emulation mapping (7a–g), and item 13 asks for effect estimates with precision including both absolute and relative measures when applicable. Official TARGET resources confirm that scope and provide protocol table and flow-diagram templates. That is real progress on the reporting-standard side and is the caveat on support: the claim is still true about practice, but “standards are missing” would be overstated after TARGET 2025. What remains open is exactly what the report names: applied reporting has not caught up; the HR remains a familiar default that survives estimator upgrades; and nothing forces a one-sentence estimand that names intervention, population induced by cloning/censoring, horizon, and intercurrent-event strategy before the first effect measure. Fourati et al. (Eur J Prev Cardiol 2026 advance article) still notes that relative measures such as hazard ratios are frequently reported and that absolute risks and risk differences at meaningful times communicate better, which is consistent with ongoing practice lag months after TARGET. No package release (TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, gfoRmulaICE, lmtp, ltmle, survtmle, concrete, riskRegression, adjustedCurves) was found that auto-emits an ICH/TARGET-style estimand sentence or demotes the HR to a supplement. opinions.rationale: Inverted-prior search did not find a solution that joins partial-interference identification to target-trial emulation in a way that closes the gaps named in the statement. Papadogeorgou et al. (2019), already cited, supplies cluster/population allocation estimands under interference; it does not supply an emulation protocol, joint-neighborhood positivity diagnostics, or clone-censor rules that keep cluster strategies feasible. Buchanan et al. (Stat Med 2022; 10.1002/sim.9427) is the closest prior art: it defines a target-trial protocol for disseminated (spillover) effects of MOUD within provider-based clusters using routinely collected data, so the “rarely joined” claim should be read as rare rather than never. That paper is an application and estimation sketch under partial interference for a specific provider-cluster exposure mapping; it does not invent cluster-level clone-censor-weighting, does not resolve non-canonical exposure mappings, and does not evaluate network mismeasurement. Lu et al. (arXiv 2604.12900, 2026) propose emulating stepped-wedge cluster randomized trials for staggered policy adoption; that covers group-level policy emulation and mentions spillovers as a shared design concern, not individual-treatment cloning that assigns impossible joint strategies. Official TARGET resources (target-guideline.org, retrieved 2026) still scope the checklist to parallel-group, individually randomized target trials, list “Emulation of a cluster target trial” as a possible future extension, and state that no extensions are currently in development, which confirms rather than repairs the reporting gap. Searches across AJE/Epidemiology/IJE/EJE/JCE/PDS/Stat Med/Biometrics, arXiv stat.ME, medRxiv, and package activity (TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, gfoRmulaICE, lmtp, ltmle, CICI, WeightIt) found no merged software that implements network/cluster-compatible clone-censor-weighting or network TMLE for TTE. Contagion/homophily/spillover non-separability and joint-neighborhood positivity remain structural; sensitivity to edge deletion is proposed in the agenda and was not found as a standard TTE tool. Vote open: prior art proposes joins in narrow settings; none solves exposure-mapping canonicity, joint positivity, network error, or cluster-compatible cloning as stated.

Transport estimators (IOSW, outcome modeling, doubly robust/TMLE, calibration) are mature for trials and increasingly documented for observational sources; that is already acknowledged by the report’s Westreich citation and does not close the problem. The open core is accounting: transporting an observational estimate stacks treatment-exchangeability on sampling-exchangeability, both largely untestable, and no standard reporting practice decomposes a discrepancy between those failure modes. Scelo et al. (Front Epidemiol 2024; 10.3389/fepid.2024.1335241) explicitly lists the internal-validity and external-validity assumption blocks side by side, notes that most are untestable, and demonstrates TMLE transport from an observational birth cohort to a registry target; that formalizes the stack and does not provide joint sensitivity or attribution. Manke-Reimers et al. (Eur J Epidemiol 2025; 10.1007/s10654-025-01217-w), already cited, maps applied transport studies and underuse of flexible estimators; a scoping review of practice is evidence the gap remains, not a solution. Adamson et al. (Pharmacoepidemiol Drug Saf 2026; 10.1002/pds.70396) offers a stepwise transportability framework for comparative effectiveness and urges sensitivity for unmeasured effect modifiers, e-values, and tipping-point analyses; that is guidance and one-parameter sensitivity, not a joint compounding account that charges residual bias to confounding versus selection/effect-modification structure. Separate sensitivity tools for unmeasured confounding and for unmeasured selection/effect modification exist; they do not identify effects when both fail in correlated ways, and the discipline rule forbids treating sensitivity as solving identification. Causal representation learning for transport that preserves effect modification (rather than predictive invariance) remains workshop/early-methods work; no 2024–2026 applied TTE package (lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, TrialEmulation, zEpid) was found that ships joint internal-plus-external fragility bounds with attribution. Queries run: transportability observational compounding/joint sensitivity; unmeasured effect modification bounds transport; Manke-Reimers and Adamson follow-ups; Scelo 2024 full text; CRL transport effect modifiers; CRAN/GitHub keyword checks for transport modules. Vote open: methods and guidance expanded; the compounding-accounting and attribution problem as stated is not solved.

The problem is framed as a presentation/practice failure after standards already exist: a reader sees a bare hazard ratio and infers an intention-to-treat contrast, while the analysis estimated a censoring-weighted per-protocol effect among grace-period–compatible (often cloned) patients. Maringe et al. (IJE 2020; 10.1093/ije/dyaa057), already cited, already makes the CCW estimand type explicit; that formalizes the distinction and does not change what applied papers headline. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement (JAMA 2025; 10.1001/jama.2025.13350) require aligned objectives, estimands, and sensitivity analyses; TARGET item structure places target-trial protocol/estimand items (6a–g) beside emulation mapping (7a–g), and item 13 asks for effect estimates with precision including both absolute and relative measures when applicable. Official TARGET resources confirm that scope and provide protocol table and flow-diagram templates. That is real progress on the reporting-standard side and is the caveat on support: the claim is still true about practice, but “standards are missing” would be overstated after TARGET 2025. What remains open is exactly what the report names: applied reporting has not caught up; the HR remains a familiar default that survives estimator upgrades; and nothing forces a one-sentence estimand that names intervention, population induced by cloning/censoring, horizon, and intercurrent-event strategy before the first effect measure. Fourati et al. (Eur J Prev Cardiol 2026 advance article) still notes that relative measures such as hazard ratios are frequently reported and that absolute risks and risk differences at meaningful times communicate better, which is consistent with ongoing practice lag months after TARGET. No package release (TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, gfoRmulaICE, lmtp, ltmle, survtmle, concrete, riskRegression, adjustedCurves) was found that auto-emits an ICH/TARGET-style estimand sentence or demotes the HR to a supplement. Vote open: standards partially codify the proposed direction; the concrete misread of weighted grace-period PP as ITT HR remains an open practice and communication problem.
